clinicalPearls: Gout is a hyperuricemic metabolic disorder in which chronic hyperuricemia leads to supersaturation and deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and connective tissue; it typically presents with episodic, intensely painful inflammatory arthritis in middle-aged-to-elderly men and postmenopausal women (Harrison 22e p.2956-2957).

The first metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases; other early targets are tarsal joints, ankles, and knees, while finger, wrist, and elbow involvement is more typical of elderly patients or advanced disease (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Flares often begin at night or in the early morning and are among the most painful conditions humans experience; affected joints rapidly become warm, red, tender, and swollen, sometimes mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis), and usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2958).

Definitive diagnosis rests on demonstrating needle-shaped MSU crystals (intracellular and extracellular) showing strong negative birefringence under compensated polarized light; synovial fluid is cloudy with leukocyte counts roughly 5000-75,000/uL (Harrison 22e p.2958-2959).

Serum urate may be normal or even low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower it by about 2 mg/dL, so a normal level during a flare does not exclude gout; historical or postflare values are more diagnostically useful (Harrison 22e p.2959).

Musculoskeletal ultrasound (double-contour sign over articular cartilage) and dual-energy CT (chemical identification of MSU) aid early diagnosis; plain radiographs in advanced tophaceous gout show well-defined erosions with sclerotic, overhanging margins and soft-tissue masses, though these are absent early (Harrison 22e p.2959).

Hyperuricemia is most often due to impaired renal urate excretion (about 90%) rather than overproduction (about 10%); roughly two-thirds of daily uric acid is eliminated renally and one-third through the gut (intestinal uricolysis by gut bacteria) (Harrison 22e p.2957).

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) is strongly age-related, with prevalence in articular tissues roughly doubling each decade after 60 and reaching nearly 50% in those over 85; most deposition is asymptomatic (Harrison 22e p.2960).

Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) most often affects the knee, then the wrist, and rarely the first MTP joint; episodes tend to last longer than gout flares (weeks to months) and may be accompanied by fever, chills, and elevated acute-phase reactants (Harrison 22e p.2960).

Chondrocalcinosis (punctate/linear radiodense deposits in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage) supports CPPD; definitive diagnosis requires rhomboid or rod-shaped weakly positively birefringent or nonbirefringent crystals in synovial fluid or tissue (Harrison 22e p.2961).

Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) crystals are extremely small and individually visible only by electron microscopy; clumps appear as nonbirefringent globules staining bright red with alizarin red S, and apatite underlies the destructive 'Milwaukee shoulder' of the elderly (Harrison 22e p.2961).

Calcium oxalate (CaOx) arthropathy is largely a disease of patients on long-term dialysis, especially with ascorbic acid supplementation, since ascorbate is metabolized to oxalate that is poorly cleared in uremia; the readily recognized crystals are bipyramidal with strong birefringence (Harrison 22e p.2962).
harrison.pathophysiology: Chronic hyperuricemia is a prerequisite for gout but not sufficient alone, since only a minority of hyperuricemic individuals ever develop disease. Humans uniquely develop gout spontaneously because of an evolutionary species-wide loss of uricase, the enzyme that converts urate to highly soluble allantoin; at physiologic pH uric acid (pKa about 5.8) exists mainly as ionized urate. An increased urate body pool leads to MSU supersaturation (favored above roughly 6.85 mg/dL) and crystal formation/deposition in joints and connective tissue, modulated by temperature, pH, intra-articular dehydration, cation concentration, and matrix proteoglycans/collagen. Hyperuricemia stems predominantly from impaired renal excretion (about 90%) and less often overproduction (about 10%); overproduction relates to increased cell turnover (hematologic malignancy, psoriasis), chemotherapy, tissue hypoxia, or inherited defects such as PRPP synthetase superactivity or HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum). Renal handling involves sodium-dependent apical reabsorption via URAT1/OAT10, basolateral GLUT9 efflux, and intestinal excretion via ABCG2. Acute flares are triggered when MSU crystals are shed from inert deposits and activate resident synovial macrophages, mast cells, and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha; neutrophil phagocytosis of crystals amplifies inflammation via a respiratory burst. Untreated, growing tophaceous MSU deposits with granulomatous inflammation produce chronic gouty arthritis with erosive deformity. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals that, like MSU, activate phagocytes and the inflammasome. Apatite deposition occurs in tissue damage (dystrophic), hypercalcemic/hyperparathyroid states (metastatic), connective tissue disease (calcinosis), and chronic renal failure (tumoral calcinosis, calciphylaxis). CaOx deposits accumulate in cartilage, synovium, bone, and viscera in chronic renal failure and primary oxalosis (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962).
additionalDifferentials: Other crystal-associated arthropathies (CPPD/pseudogout, apatite, calcium oxalate)
Rheumatoid arthritis (especially chronic tophaceous gout or pseudo-rheumatoid CPPD)
Cellulitis (pseudocellulitis appearance of an acute flare)
Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy (mimicked by severe destructive CPPD)
infectionMimics: Acute septic arthritis can closely resemble an acute crystal flare, and bacterial infection can coexist with MSU or CPP crystals in synovial fluid, so joint fluid should be Gram-stained and cultured
Acute flares with overlying erythema, warmth, and swelling can mimic cellulitis (pseudocellulitis)
nonInfectiousMimics: Rheumatoid arthritis (chronic tophaceous gout; chronic symmetric synovitis pattern of CPPD)
Spinal stenosis or crowned dens syndrome (CPPD spinal involvement)
additionalInvestigations: Synovial fluid aspiration with polarized light microscopy to identify and distinguish crystal type (MSU vs CPP); apatite is not identifiable by polarized light alone
Synovial fluid leukocyte count and microbial Gram stain and culture to exclude coexisting infection
Serum urate (interpreting with awareness it may be transiently normal during a flare)

Alizarin red S staining for calcium-containing (apatite, CaOx) crystals; electron microscopy with energy-dispersive analysis, x-ray diffraction, infrared or Raman spectroscopy for definitive apatite identification
Plain radiography (erosions with overhanging margins in gout; chondrocalcinosis in CPPD; periarticular calcification in apatite disease)
Musculoskeletal ultrasound (double-contour sign) and dual-energy CT for MSU detection

In CPPD patients under 50: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, and transferrin, plus screening for familial aggregation and metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia)
Serum creatinine, liver function tests, hemoglobin, WBC count, HbA1c, and lipids at baseline to assess comorbidities and treatment risk
redFlags: Acutely hot, swollen joint where septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically, mandating synovial fluid Gram stain and culture
Fever, chills, and elevated acute-phase reactants during a crystal flare (seen in up to 50% of acute CPPD episodes, occasionally to 40 C), which overlap with infection
Hyperuricemia in prepubertal boys, which should prompt evaluation for inherited enzyme defects (HPRT deficiency, PRPP synthetase superactivity)
CPPD arthritis in patients under 50, raising concern for an underlying metabolic disorder (e.g., hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia)
Progressive destructive large-joint disease (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) signaling severe apatite-associated joint destruction
harrison.prognosis: Typical acute gout flares are self-limited, resolving spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intercritical intervals; however, untreated recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Gout is associated with multiple cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities (obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, chronic kidney disease, urate nephrolithiasis). Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) tends to progress indolently but can cause severe pain, instability, and disability requiring joint replacement, and CaOx and chronic CPP arthropathies may progressively destroy joints (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962).
pitfalls: Assuming a normal serum urate during an acute attack excludes gout; cytokine-mediated uricosuria (e.g., IL-6) can lower it by about 2 mg/dL during flares
Failing to exclude infection: bacterial sepsis can coexist with crystals, and crystals do not rule out a septic joint
Relying on polarized light microscopy to detect apatite, whose individual crystals require electron microscopy and special stains/techniques
Overlooking a secondary metabolic cause when CPPD presents before age 50
Confusing intra-/periarticular apatite calcifications with the linear calcifications of CPPD on radiographs
Diagnosing chondrocalcinosis as CPPD without considering calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure as an alternative
harrison.severityClassification: Gout is described as a clinical continuum rather than by a formal grading scale: asymptomatic hyperuricemia; acute (episodic) gout flares with intercritical symptom-free intervals; and chronic (tophaceous) gouty arthritis with persistent synovitis, tophi, deformity, and bony destruction. Crystal-induced disease is categorized by pattern as acute (episodic) mono-, oligo-, or polyarthritis; periarticular inflammation (bursitis, tendinitis, enthesitis); tophaceous deposits; chronic destructive or chronic inflammatory arthropathy; a peculiar osteoarthritis-like form; spinal arthritis; and carpal tunnel syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2956-2957).
management: Treat acute crystal arthritis, whether urate, calcium pyrophosphate or apatite, with a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine or a systemic or intra-articular corticosteroid, aspirating and injecting the joint where feasible
For gout, lower the urate pool with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (allopurinol or febuxostat) to a crystal-dissolving target, adding a uricosuric agent if needed
Provide anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis with colchicine when commencing urate-lowering therapy

For recurrent calcium pyrophosphate disease use colchicine or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for prophylaxis, and treat underlying metabolic drivers such as haemochromatosis and hyperparathyroidism
Manage apatite-associated periarthritis with anti-inflammatories and, where indicated, needle aspiration and lavage of calcific deposits
Advise lifestyle change and review of precipitating drugs, and manage coexisting chronic kidney disease and metabolic syndrome
Aspirate any acutely inflamed joint for Gram stain and culture to exclude septic arthritis before immunosuppressive treatment
Monitor serum urate to target in gout and follow tophi and joint damage over time
